references.title: G. E. Moore, “Proof of an External World” (1939), reprinted in G. E. Moore: Selected Writings
references.support: Primary lecture text in the Selected Writings reprint; relevant passages on pp. 147, 164–166, and 168–170 state Moore’s aim, hand demonstration, three proof conditions, and response to objections. The complete original publication was not read.

references.title: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: George Edward Moore
references.support: Baldwin’s archived SEP entry, §6, discusses Moore’s common-sense position, the hand proof, the distinction between proving that external objects exist and proving that anyone knows this, and the proof’s limits regarding metaphysical independence from experience. It presents Baldwin’s interpretation, not a settled consensus.

references.title: Charles Raff, “The Point of Moore’s Proof” (2019)
references.support: Raff’s scholarly article (International Journal for the Study of Skepticism, 2019, pp. 1–27) argues from Moore’s announced aim that the performance counterexamples a presupposition of Kant’s problem; relevant passages read on pp. 1–3 and 25–26. This is an alternative interpretive argument, not a settled consensus.

references.title: Chris Tucker, “Transmission and Transmission Failure in Epistemology”
references.support: The IEP scholarly reference entry’s Moore-proof discussion distinguishes failure to transmit justification from inability to resolve doubt or be dialectically effective for a skeptical audience; it notes competing positions, including Pryor’s defense. It does not settle the debate.

references.title: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Epistemic Contextualism
references.support: Rysiew’s archived SEP entry, especially §§3.1–3.2, explains contextualism as a contested approach to skeptical arguments that allows standards for knowledge attributions to shift with context, preserving the possibility of ordinary knowledge claims. Context only; not an interpretation attributed to Moore.

references.title: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Epistemic Closure
references.support: Luper’s archived SEP entry, §5.1, describes Moore-style anti-skeptical reasoning that uses ordinary knowledge claims and closure against Cartesian skeptical hypotheses; it distinguishes this later strategy from the skeptic’s argument and from Moore’s exact 1939 hand proof.
